svg.aria-label: Eve in the middle of Bob's connection to his bank: four attacks and how TLS or HSTS defeats each

g.text: Bob’s key share
passed on, untouched
She sees both key shares go past. To get the secret she needs one of the private keys,
which never leave Bob’s laptop or the bank. Everything after the hellos is noise to her.
She learns the site’s name (the SNI), and sizes. Nothing else.
Bob’s key share
Eve’s key share!
She swaps in her own key shares, to share one secret with Bob and another with the bank.
But the bank’s CertificateVerify signs the whole conversation, which now has her key share
in it, and she can’t make a new signature without the bank’s private key.
Bob’s laptop: “signature invalid”. It hangs up.
Eve’s own certificate
She answers Bob herself, with a certificate and a key of her own, which she can sign with.
But no certificate authority will sign a certificate saying her key belongs to the bank,
so the chain doesn’t lead to any root Bob’s laptop trusts.
“Your connection is not private.” Bob stops.
http://bank… ?
https://bank…
Her last trick: catch Bob’s very first, unencrypted http:// request, and never pass on
the redirect to https://. She talks HTTPS to the bank, and plain HTTP to Bob,
and hopes he doesn’t notice the missing padlock.
HSTS (Chapter 30): the browser never sends that http:// request.

ol.li: Listening. Eve can see every packet, as she could in Chapters 19 and 21. The Diffie–Hellman exchange is designed for exactly this.
Swapping the keys. A plain Diffie–Hellman exchange can be hijacked like this: it’s the attack from the end of Chapter 31. TLS stops it with the signature.
Her own certificate. This is why certificate authorities matter: they’re the only thing that ties a name to a key.
No TLS at all. “SSL stripping” is the attack HTTPS can’t prevent by itself, because it happens before HTTPS starts. HSTS, and browsers that try https:// first, close the gap.

figure.figcaption: Eve’s four tricks, and why each one fails.
